case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a defendant’s broad plea-agreement appeal waiver bars appellate review of an alleged unconstitutional supervised-release condition and whether the waiver becomes unenforceable when the sentencing judge tells the defendant he has a right to appeal and the government does not object.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. §§ 1343 and 2 (underlying conviction context); enforceability of plea-agreement appeal waivers under federal criminal procedure and contract/waiver principles (including Rule 11 plea colloquy requirements and due-process limits on sentencing/supervised-release conditions).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues that even a generally worded appeal waiver cannot be enforced to bar review of certain fundamental sentencing errors—here, a due-process challenge to a condition of future supervised release—because such errors are not meaningfully foreseeable at the plea stage and because courts traditionally recognize exceptions beyond ineffective assistance or sentences above the statutory maximum. Petitioner also contends the waiver should not be enforced where, at sentencing, the judge affirmatively advised that petitioner had a right to appeal and the government did not object, creating (at minimum) ambiguity or a reasonable reliance problem that should defeat enforcement of the waiver in this case.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues the Fifth Circuit correctly dismissed the appeal because petitioner knowingly and voluntarily waived the right to appeal on any ground other than ineffective assistance of counsel, and that waiver applies to due-process challenges to supervised-release conditions just as it applies to other sentencing issues. The government further argues that the district court’s unobjected statement that petitioner ‘ha[d] a right to appeal’ did not modify, nullify, or waive the written appeal waiver; at most it reflected that some limited appellate rights remained, and in any event the parties’ written agreement controls.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Alito’s strongest point—that Rule 32(j) boilerplate and prosecutorial silence cannot supply mutual assent to “modify” a Rule 11 appeal waiver—is correct as far as it goes, and my disposition does not rest on any modification theory. But Justice Thomas’s categorical stance that the district court’s affirmative “you have a right to appeal” statement and the government’s silence are always legally irrelevant goes too far and is in tension with ordinary waiver/forfeiture principles and our insistence that plea waivers be enforced with clarity and fairness; Garza’s reminder that waivers are not monolithic supports a limited, record-sensitive inquiry into enforceability without creating any new categorical exception. The administrability concern Justice Kagan raises is real, yet a narrow vacatur aimed at correcting the Fifth Circuit’s categorical rule does not require prosecutors to object to every Rule 32(j) advisement; it simply requires courts to consider whether, on this record, the government’s conduct or the court’s misstatement created ambiguity or an estoppel-like unfairness in enforcing the waiver as applied. A minimal remand for that case-specific analysis best preserves plea-bargaining stability under Ricketts while avoiding mechanical enforcement when the court itself may have materially misled the defendant.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s proposal for a case-specific remand rests on fairness and ordinary waiver/forfeiture principles, but it lacks a textual hook: Rule 32(j)’s mandatory, generic advisement cannot alter the Rule 11(b)(1)(N) waiver whose original public meaning is fixed by the plea’s text and the colloquy. As Justice Alito and Justice Kagan explain, treating the government’s silence at sentencing as forfeiture would effectively require prosecutors to object to boilerplate notices to preserve a written defense—an administratively unsound, judge-made rule not grounded in the agreement or the Rules. Garza does not undermine enforcement here because it preserves challenges to the waiver’s validity, not an equitable exception whenever post-sentencing rituals create possible confusion. Class is inapposite because it addressed a guilty plea without an express waiver; where the waiver covers challenges to the sentence “on any ground,” supervised-release conditions fall within the sentence absent a showing the waiver was unknowing or involuntary.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s remand proposal is the strongest counter, but it still lacks a principled doctrinal hook: Rule 32(j)’s mandatory, generic advisement cannot create ambiguity about a waiver already fixed by the Rule 11(b)(1)(N) colloquy, and the government’s silence is not the kind of clear, intentional relinquishment that would forfeit a bargained-for waiver defense. As Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett note, turning enforceability on whether prosecutors object to routine post-sentencing boilerplate would be administratively perverse and would invite strategic gamesmanship that undermines plea-bargain finality. Garza, invoked by Roberts and others, confirms waivers are enforceable according to their terms while preserving challenges to validity; it does not authorize a case-by-case equitable inquiry keyed to post-sentencing rituals. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Class remains inapposite because Class addressed a guilty plea without an express appeal waiver, whereas this waiver’s text reaches sentencing “on any ground,” and supervised-release conditions are part of the sentence.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Alito persuasively argue that Rule 32(j)’s mandatory advisement cannot, standing alone, "modify" a Rule 11 plea waiver, and I agree we should not turn routine sentencing boilerplate into a contractual rewrite mechanism. But Chief Justice Roberts is right that the Fifth Circuit’s categorical rule—treating the judge’s affirmative “you have a right to appeal” statement plus the government’s silence as always irrelevant—conflicts with the heightened clarity/voluntariness demands that govern criminal waivers and with ordinary waiver principles that look to the whole record for reasonable understanding. The administrability concern (that prosecutors would have to object to Rule 32(j) every time) is overstated: a narrow remand standard can ask whether, in context, the defendant was affirmatively misled about what remained appealable without requiring constant objections to boilerplate. Garza’s point (noted by Roberts and Gorsuch) that waivers are not monolithic supports a tailored inquiry into whether the waiver fairly reaches this specific, later-imposed liberty-restricting condition, rather than automatic enforcement based solely on broad phrasing.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s point that a categorical rule treating the Rule 32(j) advisement and government silence as “always irrelevant” sounds too rigid, but I still don’t see a workable doctrinal pathway that wouldn’t distort Rule 11(b)(1)(N) and ordinary waiver enforcement. As Justice Alito emphasizes, Rule 32(j) is mandatory boilerplate after the plea bargain is fixed; making enforceability turn on whether the prosecutor objects to that routine advisement effectively creates an administrability trap and invites gamesmanship. Garza and Class, invoked by Justices Sotomayor and Gorsuch, reinforce that some claims can survive a waiver or a plea, but they do so via recognized channels (validity/knowingness of the waiver, not an equitable, post-sentencing “reliance” exception keyed to standard advisements). On the text, a waiver of sentencing appeals “on any ground” naturally covers supervised-release conditions as part of the sentence absent a showing the waiver itself was unknowing or involuntary, so I would enforce the waiver here.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Alito rightly stress that Rule 32(j)’s mandatory advisement cannot “modify” a Rule 11 waiver or create mutual assent after the bargain is struck; I accept that and would not rest decision on any rewriting theory. But Chief Justice Roberts persuasively identifies the Fifth Circuit’s categorical move—treating the court’s affirmative statement that the defendant has a right to appeal, coupled with the government’s silence, as always legally irrelevant—as incompatible with ordinary waiver principles that turn on a clear, knowing relinquishment and the record as a whole. Garza matters here not because it weakens waivers generally, but because it reiterates they are not monolithic and their enforceability depends on what was actually surrendered with adequate clarity; boilerplate “any ground” language should not be presumed to cover later-announced supervised-release restraints without a case-specific inquiry into understanding. On my textualist/originalist approach, the right course is a narrow vacatur and remand to assess enforceability on this record (without inventing a constitutional carve-out or a Rule 32(j) modification doctrine).

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The strongest opposing point remains Chief Justice Roberts’s fairness-and-reliance remand: I agree the Fifth Circuit should not speak in categorical absolutes that a Rule 32(j) advisement and government silence are “always irrelevant.” But on these facts, as Justice Kagan and Justice Alito stress, Rule 32(j) is mandatory, generic post-sentencing boilerplate and cannot supply mutual assent or a clear, intentional relinquishment by the government sufficient to displace an appeal waiver fixed at the Rule 11 colloquy; turning silence into forfeiture would create administrability problems and strategic incentives. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Class doesn’t move me because Class concerned the consequences of a guilty plea absent an express appeal waiver, whereas here the waiver expressly covers sentencing appeals and supervised release is part of the sentence. Garza reinforces enforcing waivers according to their terms while preserving only established avenues (e.g., challenges to the waiver’s validity), not a new equitable exception keyed to routine advisements.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s remand proposal is the strongest counter because it invokes ordinary fairness and forfeiture principles, but I still do not see a satisfactory textual or procedural hook for treating the Rule 32(j) advisement and government silence as defeating a written waiver established at the Rule 11(b)(1)(N) colloquy. As Justice Kagan and Justice Alito emphasize, Rule 32(j) is mandatory boilerplate and cannot supply mutual assent to modify the plea agreement, and converting prosecutorial silence into forfeiture would effectively require routine objections to preserve a bargained-for defense—an unworkable rule inconsistent with how we enforce waivers by their terms. Garza (as Roberts and Kagan both note) preserves challenges to the waiver’s validity, not a new equitable exception triggered whenever the judge gives the standard post-sentencing notice. Class, relied on by Justice Sotomayor and Justice Gorsuch, is distinguishable because it addressed a guilty plea without an express appeal waiver; where the waiver text reaches the sentence, supervised-release conditions are part of that sentence absent a showing the waiver was unknowing or involuntary.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Alito make the strongest point against me: Rule 32(j)’s boilerplate advisement, standing alone, cannot supply mutual assent to “modify” a Rule 11-fixed waiver, and treating the government’s silence as an across-the-board forfeiture rule would be administratively awkward. But that critique does not answer Chief Justice Roberts’s narrower concern—what is objectionable here is the Fifth Circuit’s categorical refusal to give any legal significance, in any case, to the district court’s affirmative statement that the defendant “has a right to appeal,” coupled with the government’s nonresponse, when evaluating enforceability and ambiguity in a criminal waiver regime that depends on clear and reliable procedures. Garza, as Roberts notes, underscores that appeal waivers are “not monolithic,” which supports a case-specific remand to determine whether the record (including post-sentencing statements) fairly bears on what rights the defendant reasonably understood remained, without embracing a post-sentencing “rewrite” theory. Under my pragmatic fairness lens—especially in the criminal context—I would vacate and remand to reject categorical irrelevance and require a focused inquiry into whether enforcing this waiver as applied would be procedurally fair and consistent with ordinary principles of construing ambiguity against the government as drafter.

John Roberts.reasoning: A broad appeal waiver may generally be enforced when knowing and voluntary, but we should not adopt (or allow to persist) a categorical rule that a district court’s post-sentencing advisement that the defendant “has a right to appeal,” coupled with the government’s silence, is legally irrelevant in every case; ordinary waiver and contract principles recognize modification, forfeiture, and equitable reliance in appropriate circumstances. Plea agreements are construed and enforced with special solicitude for fairness in the criminal process, and due process limits remain on sentencing, including supervised-release conditions; at minimum, the Fifth Circuit should have conducted a case-specific inquiry rather than mechanically enforcing the written waiver despite the court’s contrary instruction. A narrow disposition—vacating and remanding for the court of appeals to consider whether the government forfeited reliance on the waiver or whether the advisement created enforceable ambiguity—best preserves institutional legitimacy while respecting the general enforceability of waivers recognized in cases like Ricketts v. Adamson. This approach also avoids unnecessarily deciding the broader question whether constitutional challenges to supervised-release conditions can never be waived.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: A knowing and voluntary plea-agreement appeal waiver is enforceable according to its written terms, and nothing in the Constitution’s text or federal statutes creates a freestanding “unconstitutional supervised-release condition” exception to such waivers. This Court has recognized that even fundamental constitutional protections may be waived in plea agreements, and in that respect the waiver here—covering sentencing issues except ineffective assistance—extends to due-process challenges to supervised-release conditions. See Garza v. Idaho, 586 U.S. 232 (2019) (appeal waivers generally enforceable) and Ricketts v. Adamson, 483 U.S. 1 (1987) (enforcing plea waivers by their terms). The sentencing judge’s generic statement that the defendant had a “right to appeal,” unaccompanied by a new bargain and not incorporated into the written agreement, cannot nullify or rewrite the waiver; the parties’ written plea agreement controls.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: A knowingly and voluntarily executed appeal waiver is ordinarily enforceable according to its text, and nothing in Rule 11(b)(1)(N) or this Court’s plea-agreement cases suggests carving out a freestanding exception for later-asserted constitutional objections to supervised-release conditions when the waiver broadly covers “any ground” other than ineffective assistance. Under Ricketts v. Adamson, plea agreements are enforced like contracts, and the defendant may prospectively relinquish even important procedural protections as part of the bargain; allowing an after-the-fact due-process challenge here would undermine the finality and practical functioning of plea bargaining. The district court’s generic Rule 32(j)(1)(B) advisement that the defendant had a “right to appeal,” unaccompanied by any modification of the written agreement, does not nullify the waiver, and the government’s silence cannot reasonably be treated as assent to rewrite the parties’ bargain. Practical consequences also counsel enforcing the waiver as written: a broad “constitutional-error” escape hatch would invite routine litigation of waived sentencing issues and diminish the value of waivers to the government and to the system.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: A boilerplate appeal waiver should not be read to insulate an allegedly unconstitutional supervised-release condition from any appellate review, because sentencing—including prospective conditions—occurs after the plea and is not meaningfully foreseeable in the way trial-related errors are, and due process limits on punishment cannot be bargained away by generalized language. Consistent with Class v. United States, 583 U.S. 285 (2018), a guilty plea (and associated waivers) does not automatically foreclose constitutional challenges where enforcing the waiver would effectively authorize unlawful punishment and undermine the judiciary’s duty to ensure sentences comply with the Constitution. Separately, Rule 11’s requirement that a defendant understand the “terms of any plea-agreement provision waiving the right to appeal” is compromised when the sentencing judge affirmatively tells the defendant he has a right to appeal and the government stands silent, creating at least ambiguity and reasonable reliance that should be construed against enforcement of the waiver in this case. Given the real-world stakes of supervised-release conditions for vulnerable defendants, appellate review is necessary to ensure constitutional compliance and meaningful access to justice.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: A knowing and voluntary plea-agreement appeal waiver is generally enforceable according to its terms, and nothing in Rule 11 authorizes a district court to unilaterally revise that bargain after the plea is accepted; plea agreements are construed and enforced as contracts subject to ordinary waiver principles. The waiver’s broad text covers challenges to “any” sentencing component, and supervised-release conditions are part of the sentence; absent an express carve-out, a constitutional challenge to such a condition is still an “appeal” the defendant agreed to forgo, consistent with this Court’s treatment of plea bargains as binding agreements. The sentencing judge’s generic Rule 32(j) advice that the defendant “has a right to appeal,” without a written modification or mutual assent, does not nullify the previously accepted waiver, and the government’s silence does not amount to forfeiture of the waiver’s benefit. Ricketts v. Adamson supports enforcing the plea bargain as written, while Garza v. Idaho confirms that waivers do not erase all appellate rights but does not create a categorical exception permitting review here.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: A plea-agreement appeal waiver should be enforced according to its terms, but only when the waiver is knowing, voluntary, and clearly covers the specific claim; courts should not presume a relinquishment of constitutional objections to future, unknown supervised-release conditions absent unmistakable clarity. When the sentencing judge affirmatively advises the defendant he has a right to appeal and the government stands silent, ordinary waiver/contract principles and Rule 11’s demand for a clear record of understanding cut against enforcing the waiver to foreclose review of an allegedly unconstitutional condition. This approach respects separation-of-powers limits by ensuring sentencing courts remain bound by constitutional constraints and avoids converting boilerplate waivers into implied licenses for unlawful conditions. Class v. United States supports the baseline that a guilty plea does not, without clear relinquishment, extinguish certain constitutional challenges; the same clarity principle applies a fortiori to appeal waivers aimed at future sentencing conditions.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: A knowing and voluntary appellate waiver in a plea agreement is generally enforceable and should be construed according to its terms, and nothing in Rule 32(j)’s standard advisement requires treating a sentencing judge’s generic statement that a defendant “has a right to appeal” as nullifying the parties’ written bargain. Under Garza v. Idaho, a waiver does not eliminate all appellate rights and the government may still invoke the waiver on appeal; here, the waiver’s breadth reasonably encompasses sentencing issues, including supervised-release conditions, absent a recognized exception such as a sentence above the statutory maximum or ineffective assistance affecting the plea. Practical workability and institutional concerns also favor enforcing clear waivers to preserve the stability of plea bargaining, while leaving the defendant alternative avenues (e.g., as-applied challenges later or collateral review where available) for truly unforeseeable constitutional defects. The government’s failure to object at sentencing to a routine advisement, given the timing and purpose of Rule 32(j), does not amount to a modification of the written agreement or a relinquishment of the government’s right to enforce the waiver on appeal.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: A broad, knowing, and voluntary appeal waiver is enforceable according to its text, and nothing in the original public meaning of the relevant procedural framework or this Court’s precedents makes due-process challenges to supervised-release conditions categorically nonwaivable. Garza v. Idaho confirms that appeal waivers are not “monolithic,” but it preserves only the ability to contest the waiver’s own validity (e.g., unknowing or involuntary) and expressly declines to constitutionalize additional exceptions; the Fifth Circuit’s enforcement here is therefore consistent with methodological restraint and precedent. The sentencing judge’s generic statement that the defendant had a “right to appeal,” without more, does not modify the written plea agreement or render the waiver unknowing where Rule 11 procedures established the waiver’s terms and the government’s silence cannot rewrite the parties’ bargain. Absent a showing that the waiver itself was invalid, the proper course is to enforce it and dismiss the appeal.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: A sweeping appeal waiver cannot be read to foreclose appellate review of a supervised-release condition alleged to be unconstitutional, because due process limits on punishment are not ordinary, foreseeable “sentencing issues” at the plea stage and enforcing the waiver here would undermine procedural fairness in the imposition of future deprivations of liberty. Separately, when the district court advises at sentencing that the defendant “has a right to appeal,” Rule 32(j)(1)(B) creates a concrete risk of reasonable reliance; at minimum, courts should conduct a case-specific inquiry into whether the government’s silence and the court’s advisement render enforcement inequitable under ordinary waiver/estoppel principles, rather than applying a categorical rule that the written waiver always controls. That approach is consistent with this Court’s insistence that appellate waivers do not extinguish all appellate rights and that courts must safeguard meaningful review where fundamental rights are implicated, see Garza v. Idaho, 586 U.S. 232 (2019). Because the Fifth Circuit treated the judge’s advisement and the government’s non-objection as legally irrelevant, I would vacate and remand for consideration of enforceability under those principles rather than dismissing outright.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a defendant’s broad appeal waiver in a federal plea agreement bars appellate review of a later-imposed supervised-release condition challenged on constitutional/due-process grounds, and whether the district court’s end-of-sentencing statement that the defendant “has a right to appeal” (with no government objection) makes the waiver unenforceable.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 3742 (statutory framework for federal sentencing appeals) and the Fifth Amendment Due Process Clause (as the asserted basis for challenging a supervised-release condition), with enforcement governed by plea-agreement waiver doctrine.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues that (1) even a generally worded appeal waiver cannot categorically foreclose appellate review of certain serious sentencing errors—particularly constitutional/due-process challenges to supervised-release conditions imposed for the future—because such claims were not meaningfully knowable at the time of the plea and courts should recognize broader exceptions than the Fifth Circuit’s narrow approach; and (2) the waiver should not be enforced where the sentencing judge affirmatively told petitioner he had a right to appeal and the government did not object, because that advisement reasonably undermines or modifies the waiver’s operation (or at least prevents dismissal based solely on the waiver).
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues that petitioner knowingly and voluntarily waived the right to appeal on any ground other than ineffective assistance of counsel, that the waiver by its terms covers petitioner’s challenge to a supervised-release condition (even if framed as due process), and that courts should not create additional exceptions beyond the waiver’s text; the judge’s generic statement that petitioner had a right to appeal did not nullify or modify the written waiver—especially absent any express government agreement—and, in any event, the statement can be read as accurate because some issues (e.g., ineffective assistance) remain outside the waiver.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson make the strongest fairness point: supervised-release conditions can be unknown at the plea stage, and a due-process label highlights the continuing restraints they impose. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, Garza v. Idaho rejects “monolithic” waivers only to preserve challenges to waiver validity and other unwaived claims—not to create a freestanding constitutional carveout for sentencing objections recast as due process. The district court’s generic Rule 32 advisement that the defendant “has a right to appeal,” without any clear mutual assent to modify the plea, is plausibly accurate given residual avenues (including contesting enforceability) and cannot, consistent with administrability and our plea-bargain precedents (cf. Ricketts), rewrite the parties’ allocation of risk. A narrow holding enforcing this waiver on these facts still leaves room for defendants to prevail in cases of ambiguity, affirmative misadvice tied to the waiver, or involuntariness.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Jackson and Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that later-imposed supervised-release conditions may be “unknowable” at the plea stage and thus, as a matter of due process, should remain appealable. But under the waiver’s ordinary meaning—waiving any appeal from the sentence “on any ground” except ineffective assistance—the defendant assumed the risk of unknown sentencing components, and relabeling a challenge as “constitutional” cannot add an extra-textual carveout absent ambiguity or involuntariness in the waiver itself. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan explain, Garza v. Idaho shows only that waivers are not “monolithic” because some claims survive (including waiver validity), not that courts should invent a general due-process exception to a knowing waiver; likewise, the judge’s generic Rule 32 advisement cannot unilaterally modify the bargain, and can be true insofar as residual claims remain. Nothing in § 3742 or our precedents makes appellate review of supervised-release conditions categorically nonwaivable, so enforcing the agreement as written best fits the Constitution’s original meaning and the text the parties adopted.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Jackson and Justice Sotomayor press the most serious point: supervised-release conditions may be unknown at the plea and can be quite burdensome, so due process should preserve some appellate backstop. But under the waiver’s text—appeal waived “on any ground” save ineffective assistance—the defendant assumed the risk of later sentencing components, including supervised release, and our ordinary waiver doctrine does not turn on whether a future sentencing detail was fully predictable. Garza, as Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, shows only that waivers are not “monolithic” because some claims (including waiver validity) remain; it does not authorize courts to create an extra-textual constitutional carveout for sentencing claims relabeled “due process.” Finally, the district judge’s generic Rule 32-style statement that the defendant “has a right to appeal,” and the Government’s silence, cannot be treated as mutual modification of the written bargain and is readily true insofar as residual appellate avenues (e.g., challenging the waiver’s enforceability) still exist.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan make the administrability point that a generic Rule 32 advisement cannot “rewrite” a written waiver and can be true insofar as some appellate avenues remain, and I accept that as a general proposition. But that contract frame assumes the defendant knowingly assumed the risk of later-imposed, prospective supervised-release restraints that were not meaningfully knowable at the plea—especially where the sentencing judge affirmatively told him he “has a right to appeal” and the Government stood silent, which bears directly on whether the waiver is being applied in a knowing and fair way in operation. Garza v. Idaho, as Justice Jackson emphasizes, undercuts treating the waiver as a monolithic bar and supports at least a narrow inquiry/remand into enforceability and scope in this posture, rather than categorical dismissal of a due-process challenge to ongoing punishment. Ricketts v. Adamson’s bargain-enforcement principle remains important, but it does not justify insulating potentially unlawful, forward-looking conditions from any meaningful appellate backstop where the record suggests reasonable confusion about retained appellate rights.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson make the strongest fairness point: supervised-release conditions can be unknowable at the plea stage and may raise serious constitutional concerns, especially given the judge’s generic Rule 32 appeal advisement. But under the waiver’s sweeping text—appeals of the sentence “on any ground” except ineffective assistance—the parties allocated the risk of later-imposed sentencing components, and Garza (as the Chief and Justice Gorsuch stress) preserves challenges to waiver validity/enforceability rather than creating a free-floating due-process carveout for any sentencing claim relabeled constitutional. I do not read the judge’s advisement, plus Government silence, as a modification of the bargain absent clear mutual assent; it can be accurate because some appellate avenues remain (including arguing the waiver is not knowing/voluntary as applied). A categorical supervised-release exception would be hard to administer and would undermine statutory and plea-bargain coherence where the text already provides the limiting principle: enforce unless traditional waiver defects are shown.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press a serious due-process concern: some supervised-release conditions may be unknowable at the plea stage and can be highly intrusive. But under the text of this waiver—covering sentencing appeals “on any ground” except ineffective assistance—the ordinary meaning allocates that risk unless the defendant shows a traditional defect in waiver enforceability (ambiguity, involuntariness, or breach), and I agree with the Chief Justice that a generic Rule 32 advisement cannot silently amend the parties’ written bargain. Garza v. Idaho, as Justice Kagan emphasizes, supports allowing a defendant to file a notice and litigate waiver validity/scope, not creating a free-floating constitutional carveout that nullifies an otherwise valid waiver whenever a claim is styled “due process.” Without record evidence that this particular waiver was unknowing or that the court’s advisement induced reliance sufficient to undermine voluntariness, I would enforce the agreement as written.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Jackson and Justice Sotomayor make the best fairness point: some supervised-release conditions are difficult to anticipate at the plea stage and can impose serious prospective restraints, so due process should require at least some backstop. But under my institutionalist, precedent-respecting approach, that concern goes to (1) whether the waiver was knowing/voluntary or (2) whether there was ambiguity or government breach—not to creating a categorical constitutional carveout from a waiver that expressly bars sentencing appeals “on any ground” except ineffective assistance, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize. Garza v. Idaho supports that line: it rejects treating waivers as “monolithic” only insofar as defendants can still file a notice and litigate waiver enforceability or excluded claims; it does not authorize courts to bypass a valid waiver simply because the sentencing claim is labeled “due process.” Nor does the district court’s generic Rule 32 appeal advisement, coupled with government silence, supply the clear mutual assent needed to modify the written bargain; it is readily read as accurate given residual appellate avenues, so I would enforce the waiver here while leaving room for traditional voluntariness/misleading-record challenges in a truly different case.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s due-process framing most directly challenges my position, but it ultimately targets the wisdom of allocating risk rather than the waiver’s enforceability under its text. As the Chief Justice notes, the district court’s generic Rule 32(j) advisement that the defendant “has a right to appeal” cannot unilaterally modify a written waiver absent mutual assent, and it is readily accurate given residual avenues (e.g., ineffective assistance or challenges to voluntariness/scope). Garza v. Idaho, which Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson invoke, supports treating waivers as “not monolithic” only insofar as it preserves litigation over waiver validity or excluded claims; it does not create a freestanding constitutional carveout for sentencing challenges relabeled as due process. On an original public meaning and administrability view, a waiver of sentencing appeals “on any ground” (except ineffective assistance) encompasses later-imposed supervised-release conditions unless traditional defects (ambiguity, involuntariness, breach) are shown.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s administrability point seriously: a generic Rule 32 advisement ordinarily cannot unilaterally modify a written plea waiver, and Garza v. Idaho does not create a free-floating constitutional carveout for any claim labeled “due process.” But that does not resolve my narrower concern: whether enforcing this waiver to foreclose any review of a later-imposed, forward-looking supervised-release condition—one the defendant could not meaningfully anticipate at the plea—remains knowing, intelligent, and procedurally fair on this record, particularly where the sentencing judge affirmatively said he “has a right to appeal” and the Government’s silence reasonably reinforced that understanding (as Justice Sotomayor stresses). Justice Kagan is right that the advisement can be “true” in the abstract because some claims survive, yet due process is not satisfied by abstract truth if the court’s statement predictably induces forfeiture of the only realistic avenue to test the legality of an ongoing restraint. Under my pragmatic, fairness-focused approach, the proper disposition is at least a remand for a focused inquiry into waiver scope/enforceability as applied to this unforeseeable condition, rather than categorical dismissal.

John Roberts.reasoning: A knowing and voluntary appellate-rights waiver in a federal plea agreement is generally enforceable according to its terms, and nothing in 18 U.S.C. § 3742 creates a nonwaivable entitlement to sentencing-appeal review for supervised-release conditions simply because they are framed as Fifth Amendment due-process objections. Under plea-agreement doctrine, waivers are construed and enforced like contracts, and modification requires mutual assent; a district court’s generic Rule 32(j)(1)(B) advisement that the defendant “has a right to appeal,” without more, cannot unilaterally rewrite the parties’ bargain, nor does the government’s silence supply an agreement to amend. Consistent with institutional-legitimacy concerns and the preference for narrow rulings, the better course is to enforce the written waiver while recognizing it leaves some avenues open (e.g., ineffective assistance of counsel), so the judge’s statement can be read as accurate rather than as vitiating the waiver. Ricketts v. Adamson supports enforcing plea bargains as written absent a basis to set them aside, and nothing here justifies creating a broader constitutional exception to appeal waivers than the agreement’s text.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The appeal waiver should be enforced according to its text: by knowingly and voluntarily agreeing to waive appeal “on any ground” (save ineffective assistance), petitioner relinquished statutory appellate review under 18 U.S.C. § 3742, including challenges to supervised-release conditions later imposed as part of the sentence. Plea agreements are to be construed and enforced by their terms, and this Court has treated them as binding bargains rather than vehicles for judicially created exceptions untethered to the parties’ agreement. The district court’s generic end-of-sentencing statement that petitioner “has a right to appeal” cannot rewrite the written waiver absent mutual assent; at most it is accurate insofar as some claims (e.g., ineffective assistance) remain outside the waiver, and the government’s silence does not supply contractual modification or relinquishment. Any due-process objection to the supervised-release condition therefore falls within the bargained-for waiver and is barred.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Textually and as a matter of settled plea-waiver doctrine, a defendant may knowingly and voluntarily waive the statutory right to appeal a sentence under 18 U.S.C. § 3742, and a broadly worded waiver that preserves only ineffective-assistance claims encompasses a due-process attack on supervised-release conditions imposed as part of the sentence. Nothing in the Due Process Clause creates a categorical, nonwaivable entitlement to direct appellate review of future-facing supervised-release conditions, and Class v. United States confirms only that a guilty plea alone does not bar certain constitutional claims absent an explicit waiver—here there was an explicit waiver. The district court’s generic end-of-sentencing statement that the defendant “has a right to appeal” does not rewrite or rescind the written agreement, especially where it can be understood as referring to residual issues outside the waiver (e.g., ineffective assistance), and contract-like principles in plea cases counsel enforcing the parties’ written bargain. Enforcing such waivers promotes finality and preserves the practical benefits to law enforcement and the public obtained through negotiated pleas, consistent with Ricketts v. Adamson’s emphasis on holding defendants and the government to their plea agreements.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: A broad appeal waiver should not be read to foreclose appellate review of later-imposed supervised-release conditions that are challenged as unconstitutional or fundamentally violative of due process, because such future-facing restrictions are not meaningfully knowable at the time of the plea and implicate access to courts to remedy unlawful punishment under 18 U.S.C. § 3742 and the Fifth Amendment. Garza v. Idaho rejects the notion that an appeal waiver is a “monolithic end to all appellate rights” and confirms that defendants retain the ability to contest enforceability and other unwaiveable claims, which supports recognizing at least a constitutional-floor exception for supervised-release conditions. Separately, when the sentencing judge affirmatively tells the defendant he “has a right to appeal” and the Government stands silent, basic fairness and contract/waiver doctrine counsel against enforcing the waiver to summarily dismiss—at minimum requiring a remand to determine whether the waiver remained knowing and voluntary in operation. Given the practical stakes for vulnerable defendants subject to intrusive supervised-release terms, courts should preserve a narrow pathway for review of constitutionally suspect conditions rather than treating the waiver as categorically dispositive.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: A knowing and voluntary appellate waiver is generally enforceable according to its text, and nothing in 18 U.S.C. § 3742 creates a nonwaivable right to appeal sentencing issues; plea agreements are construed like contracts so long as basic fairness is preserved. The waiver here—covering any appeal except ineffective assistance—encompasses a constitutional/due-process challenge to a later-imposed supervised-release condition because the claim targets the sentence and the parties allocated that risk in the bargain, consistent with Ricketts v. Adamson’s emphasis on enforcing plea terms. Garza v. Idaho reinforces that waivers are not “monolithic,” but it treats the key limits as challenges to the waiver’s validity (unknowing/involuntary) and other unwaivable claims; petitioner’s argument goes to the merits of sentencing, not to whether the waiver itself was defective. The district court’s generic end-of-sentencing statement that the defendant “has a right to appeal,” without more and without an express governmental relinquishment, does not modify the written waiver and can be read as accurate because some appellate avenues (e.g., ineffective assistance or waiver validity) remain.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Nothing in 18 U.S.C. § 3742 guarantees an appeal in the face of a knowing and voluntary plea waiver; the statute creates a right to seek review, but a defendant may bargain away the exercise of that right as part of a plea agreement. This Court has repeatedly treated plea agreements as enforceable bargains in which defendants may waive even constitutional protections, and we do not ordinarily invent extra-textual carveouts that let one party keep the benefits while shedding the burdens. Ricketts v. Adamson confirms that plea bargains are enforced according to their terms, and Garza v. Idaho—while requiring counsel to file a notice of appeal on request—does not hold that waived issues become appealable, only that the waiver is not an absolute bar to filing. The district court’s generic end-of-sentencing remark that the defendant “has a right to appeal,” unaccompanied by any express modification accepted by both parties, cannot rewrite the written agreement (and can be read as accurate insofar as some claims like ineffective assistance remain outside the waiver).

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: A knowing and voluntary appeal waiver in a federal plea agreement is generally enforceable according to its terms, and nothing in 18 U.S.C. § 3742 creates a categorical right to appeal sentencing issues that overrides such waivers. Consistent with Ricketts v. Adamson, plea agreements operate as bargained-for exchanges that courts should enforce to preserve workability and the integrity of the criminal-justice system; carving out a broad constitutional/due-process exception for later-imposed supervised-release conditions would invite litigation over the scope of “constitutional” labeling and undermine the waiver’s practical value. The district court’s generic Rule 32(j)(1)(B)-style statement that the defendant “has a right to appeal,” without more, does not modify the written agreement or render the waiver unenforceable, especially where some issues remain appealable notwithstanding the waiver (e.g., ineffective assistance), as reflected in Garza v. Idaho’s recognition that waivers do not extinguish all appellate rights. Given precedent, institutional stability, and administrability, the waiver bars this appeal and the Fifth Circuit’s enforcement should be affirmed.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The text of the plea agreement’s appeal waiver—waiving appeal on any ground other than ineffective assistance—covers a challenge to a supervised-release condition imposed as part of the sentence, and 18 U.S.C. § 3742 does not supply a nonwaivable entitlement to appellate review in the face of a knowing and voluntary waiver. Consistent with enforcing plea terms according to their written scope, see Ricketts v. Adamson, 483 U.S. 1 (1987), a due-process label does not by itself create an extra-textual exception where the waiver is broad and the claim concerns the sentence. The district court’s generic end-of-sentencing statement that the defendant “has a right to appeal” does not modify the parties’ written agreement absent an express alteration or assent by the Government, and it can be read as accurate given that some matters (e.g., ineffective assistance) remain outside the waiver, cf. Garza v. Idaho, 586 U.S. 232 (2019). A narrower rule preserves methodological consistency: enforce waivers as written while leaving traditional contract defenses for true ambiguity, lack of voluntariness, or government breach.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: A broad appeal waiver cannot be enforced to categorically bar review of a later-imposed supervised-release condition when the defendant raises a serious Fifth Amendment due-process objection to a prospective restriction that was not meaningfully knowable at the time of the plea; Garza v. Idaho recognizes appeal waivers are not a “monolithic end to all appellate rights” and that at least some claims remain unwaivable or outside a waiver’s enforceable scope. Procedural fairness concerns are heightened where the district court, at sentencing, affirmatively advised the defendant he “has a right to appeal,” and the government’s silence reasonably reinforces confusion about the waiver’s operation—undermining the showing that the waiver is being applied in a knowing, intelligent way as required for waivers of constitutional rights. Consistent with 18 U.S.C. § 3742’s framework allowing sentencing appeals and the Due Process Clause, the appropriate course is to permit appellate review (or at minimum remand for the court of appeals to consider enforceability under ordinary contract/waiver doctrines in light of the judge’s advisement), rather than dismiss solely on the waiver’s breadth.
